newsitem.title: CHINA: INTERVIEW-Chinese develop a taste for red meat.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Chinese develop a taste for red meat.

text.p: Chinese consumers are discovering the delights of eating beef, even as consumers in the developed world are starting to avoid red meat for the sake of their health and girths, a U.S. marketing executive said.

"When we see the growth in income in China, and the number of people, we can't help but believe there has got to be quite a bright future here for U.S. meat products," said Bryant Wadsworth, of the U.S. Meat Export Federation.

Global consumption and production of red meat would be declining if China was taken out of the equation, Wadsworth, the federation's executive vice president of international programmes, told Reuters in an interview.
Wadsworth was in Shanghai to attend celebrations late on Monday for the opening of a federation representative office in China's biggest city.
"If you look at the overall beef picture, you see quite stagnant consumption and stagnant production," he said.
"If you took China out of the picture, it would be declining pretty rapidly on both the consumption and the production side. Health concerns could be a part of that," Wadsworth said.
"China is producing and consuming large amounts of beef and pork each year -- production is increasing and consumption is increasing.
"But their production is not keeping up with consumption so they are having to fill the gap of several tens of thousands of tonnes each year by importing, and I think that will increase," he said.
Figures provided by the federation show China's beef consumption grew to an estimated 4.299 million tonnes in 1996, from 4.062 million in 1995, and 3.199 million in 1994.
The figures, from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, projected 1997 consumption would hit 4.605 million tonnes.

China's Ministry of Agriculture has estimated per capita consumption of all meats will grow to 55 kg (121.25 lb) by 2000, up from just five kg (11 lb) in 1990. The USDA put 1996 per capita consumption at 47 kg.
The ministry puts total meat production at 50 million tonnes in 1996, and says it will reach 52 to 55 million tonnes by 2000, and 65 to 70 million by 2010.
Wadsworth said he believes China's pork consumption has reached its upper limit, but beef consumption still has a long way to go.
"China's role in stimulating world beef trade is small but we would expect it to become more prominent," he said.
The federation sees China's taste for beef riding on particular items, he said, as imports of U.S. beef products are now primarily variety meats, or offal.
"This is very good for us because we have a hard time selling those products at home -- like U.S. chicken producers send their feet over here, that they would just throw away otherwise," he said.
China's total beef imports in 1996 were 25,838 tonnes, significantly up on 1995's 17,563 tonnes, official figures show.

These figures were probably an understatement, the U.S. agriculture attache in Beijing said in a report last week, as significant quantities of meat are moved into China from Hong Kong outside official import channels.

In 1996, Hong Kong imported more than 77,000 tonnes of pork and more than 40,000 tonnes of beef, the attache's report to Washington said, adding that traders believed at least half of it moved into China.
